data.title: Another wildfire races through Southern California, prompting mass evacuation orders
data.description:
California News
breaking

Wildfire races through SoCal, burning homes as mass evacuations ordered

By
Ross O'Keefe
Published Oct. 16, 2026, 1:06 p.m. PT

See more of our coverage in your search results.

A wildfire in Orange County exploded in size Friday, forcing evacuation orders as it torched homes and threatened dozens more, growing to over 460 acres in just three hours.

The Norte Fire broke out around 11:30 a.m. in the San Clemente area and quickly grew to at least 50 acres by around noon, according to the Orange County Fire Authority and CalFire.

By 1:12 p.m., the fire blew up to 250 acres and had 0% containment. The OCFA confirmed on X the blaze had “impacted” four homes off Via La Mira in San Juan Capistrano.

As of 2:41 p.m., the fire has burned 465 acres, according to CalFire.

Aerial footage from KTLA showed several homes burning in the San Clemente area as the fire approached many more.

“Crews are aggressively attacking the fire from the ground and air. Please continue to avoid the area,” Cal Fire wrote in a 12:30 p.m. update.

Evacuation orders have been issued for San Juan Zones 4, 5, and 10 as well as San Clemente Zones 12 and 13.

Heat, strong winds, and dry conditions were fueling the blaze as firefighters and aerial support worked to stop its spread.

Smoke from the fire prompted the Capistrano Unified School District to urge students to stay indoors due to the smoke.

San Clemente Mayor Rick Loeffler told KTLA the city had been making preparations for a fire.

“We actually instituted a goat program about a year ago, a pilot program to have goats start clearing our hillsides,” he said.

“The county supplied a pumpkin tank at the top of our ridge, which allows helicopters to come in and resupply their water quickly.”

The fire is one of several scorching SoCal right now, as fire officials are also dealing with the Bryson Fire in Malibu, the Henderson Fire near Camp Pendleton, and the Peak Fire in Azusa.

Ongoing Red Flag Warnings in effect across much of Los Angeles and Ventura counties have signalled ideal conditions for fires to break out.

Officials advise those in the community to avoid the area of the fire. There are no reported injuries. The cause of the fire is under investigation.

data.title: Trump suggests White House press secretary Katie Zacharia may be better off leaving
data.description:
Trump casts doubt on press secretary Zacharia's future

WILL WEISSERT and SEUNG MIN KIM
Updated Fri, October 16, 2026 at 5:21 PM UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Trump

1 of 2
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia arrives with President Donald Trump at Glacier Park International Airport, Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, in Kalispell, Mont. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon) (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump signaled Friday that his embattled new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, may be on her way out — a mere week after he picked her for the post.

Speaking to reporters on the White House lawn as he left for a rally in Georgia, Trump said he'd spoken to Zacharia and that he felt she didn't deserve what he called negative media coverage.

Recounting what was said in that conversation, the president added, "I told her, 'I think you're better off being happy.'"

Advertisement

"We're talking about -- I want her to have a good life. I don't want her to have a life like she's led the last three days," Trump said.

He added, "I said, 'Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this.'"

The president said he'd make a final determination later, perhaps after his campaign travel, adding, "When I get back, we're gonna talk."

He also said, "I told Katie, in my opinion, she was treated very unfairly."

Trump noted that Zacharia has been "brutalized by the media."

data.title: Amber Guyger released on parole after serving 7 years for Botham Jean’s murder
data.description:
Former Dallas police Officer Amber Guyger walked free from prison Friday morning after serving seven years behind bars for the murder of Botham Jean. 

Guyger, 38, shot 26-year-old Jean inside his apartment in September 2018. He had been sitting on his couch eating ice cream when Guyger, who was off-duty but still in uniform, opened the door. She said she mistook Jean’s apartment for her own and believed he was a burglar. He lived on the fourth floor; she lived on the third.

She was convicted of murder and sentenced to 10 years in prison in 2019, but was granted parole earlier this month. Guyger was released after 10 a.m. from the Christina Melton Crain Unit in Gatesville. CBS reported live from the unit, but news cameras didn’t capture her release. 

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Texas Department of Criminal Justice officials said Guyger was released into community supervision.

Guyger was required to travel directly to her new residence and check in immediately with her parole officer, according to Texas parole requirements. 

She was allowed to take home personal items accumulated while in prison and will either wear state-issued civilian clothes or clothes brought to her by visitors or the people picking her up. Guyger walked out with her parole papers, a temporary ID and a prepaid debit card or check for money left in her inmate trust account.

Guyger was denied parole in 2024 after the state parole board said she was not rehabilitated or ready for release. 

Her request was granted this time after a review found her record showed no documented pattern of violence, that she maintained a “satisfactory institutional adjustment” and that she completed a treatment plan that “should enhance” her chances of obtaining — and keeping — a full-time job, a Texas Board of Pardons and Paroles spokesperson said in early October. 

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The board has several options for what type of parole to grant an inmate, a vote that depends on individual circumstances and the inmate’s behavior during time served.

Guyger was granted direct release with no additional restrictions beyond her parole conditions, the least restrictive form of parole approval a Texas inmate can receive. 

The decision to release her sparked a new wave of interest and emotion around the case, which drew international attention, sparked protests and led Texas lawmakers to pass the Botham Jean Act.

Also known as Bo’s Law, the statute requires officers to keep their body cameras on for the entirety of their participation in an investigation. That same year, Dallas renamed part of South Lamar Street for Jean.

“The past eight years have been an incredibly traumatic and painful experience for Botham Jean’s family,” the family said in an official statement released in early October. “The loss of Botham has left our family forever dismembered, and that is something we continue to live with every day.” 

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Guyger’s parole conditions were not released, but her trial attorney, who no longer represents her, told The Dallas Morning News after the parole vote that she has a job that will keep her out of the public life and a living arrangement that will stay private. 

“She’s hopeful, optimistic, tremendously remorseful,” attorney Robert Rogers said. “That’s probably something she’ll always live with.”

Parole conditions

Most parolees must follow the same basic set of rules, alongside any special conditions decided by the parole board, which are typically kept confidential. 

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Guyger will have to follow her parole conditions until September 2029.

Failure to follow the conditions can result in parole revocation, which sends the inmate back to prison for the remainder of their sentence, or lesser sanctions such as curfew adjustments or brief incarceration in a facility designed for parolees.

State law requires all parolees to get permission from their parole officer if they want to change residences or leave the state. They must be working or in school, and they have to check in regularly with their parole officer, submit monthly education or work reports, and submit to random alcohol and drug testing and unannounced searches. 

They’re forbidden from breaking the law, owning or being around firearms and ammunition, and from contacting the victim directly or indirectly. They must make restitution payments and reimburse the prison for some educational programs.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Guyger still faces a judgment of nearly $100 million from a federal civil suit connected to Jean’s murder.

data.title: Kristi Noem no longer serving as Trump envoy to Shield of the Americas
data.description:
First on CBS
Politics

Kristi Noem no longer serving as Trump envoy to Shield of the Americas

By
Olivia Gazis
Olivia Gazis covers intelligence and international security matters for CBS News. Twice Emmy-nominated, she has traveled worldwide with the secretary of state and contributes reporting on intelligence, foreign policy and other security topics across CBS News broadcast, radio, online and streaming platforms.
Read Full Bio
Olivia Gazis

October 15, 2026 / 5:00 PM EDT / CBS News

Add CBS News on Google

Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem is no longer serving as the Trump administration's special envoy for the Shield of the Americas initiative, a State Department official said Thursday, though she remains involved in the administration's efforts to coordinate security cooperation across the Western Hemisphere.

"Kristi Noem's envoy status expired last month and she is no longer in the role," a State Department official told CBS News Thursday. "She is now a senior advisor to Deputy Secretary Landau and continues to work on the Shield of the Americas portfolio." 

The Shield of the Americas is a coalition made up of the United States and several Caribbean and Latin American countries established by the Trump administration earlier this year to cooperate on economic matters, anti-cartel enforcement and other issues.

Noem's envoy designation expired just before the United Nations General Assembly last month in New York, where she continued participating in diplomatic meetings connected to the initiative. 

On Sept. 22, she met with Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa, whose government publicly identified her as the special envoy for the Shield of the Americas. She also attended a gathering of Shield of the Americas leaders hosted by President Trump, where he publicly acknowledged her work. 

"I want to thank Kristi Noem for doing a really terrific job," Mr. Trump said during his remarks.

Noem was appointed special envoy for the Shield of the Americas in March, after she was removed as homeland security secretary amid mounting scrutiny of her management of the department and the influence of her adviser, Corey Lewandowski. 

Her transition to the envoy role coincided with a five-country tour of Latin America and the Caribbean in March, much of which took place as she completed her tenure as homeland security secretary. Lewandowski appeared in photographs during those visits, though the State Department later clarified he had no formal position at the department. 

Her public activities in the envoy role appear to have been limited, and included meeting Noboa in Quito on March 25, holding discussions with Ecuadorian and Colombian diplomats in Washington in September, and participating in meetings with regional leaders on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly. 

This story published first on CBS News at 5:00 p.m. on Oct. 15, 2026.

data.title: Power struggle erupts in Trump's White House as specter of midterm losses loom
data.description:
Power struggle erupts in Trump's White House as midterm losses loom

Nancy Cook,Natalie Allison,Isaac Arnsdorf and Katherine Doyle, (c) 2026 , The Washington Post
Updated Fri, October 16, 2026 at 9:00 AM UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

White House aides, who have kept clashes muted during President Donald Trump's second term, have begun jostling more openly for power as they brace for widespread midterm election losses and internal upheaval, according to interviews with 20 staffers, advisers and people close to the president.

The interviews, most of which were conducted on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel machinations, paint a picture of infighting that has started to resemble the pitched battles of Trump's first term.

Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post.

Advertisement

Believing that Chief of Staff Susie Wiles might step down after the election, a handful of Trump aides, including Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, top housing official Bill Pulte and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, have begun angling for the position should it become available.

Wiles has given no indication to aides or allies that she plans to leave. Still, high-level White House staffers frequently cycle out of their stressful jobs after 18 months to two years, and Trump had four chiefs of staff, including an acting one, during his first term.

The past week in the White House has been "the new Wild Wild West," one Trump ally said.

The jockeying started in earnest last week after Trump first reached out to Katie Zacharia about joining the administration as the new White House press secretary, a move he made without consulting Wiles, according to four people familiar with the decision. The unilateral action by the president was viewed internally as undermining Wiles, creating the impression of a less-disciplined operation and an unsettled center of power inside the West Wing.

For longtime observers of Trump's inner circle, the friction this week harks back to his first term, when shifting factions of aides and family members vied for power and undermined one another in the process - a pattern this White House has mostly avoided, until now.

Compounding the uncertainty is the president, who has told allies he feels frustrated that no one is publicly defending him as vociferously as he would like 18 days before the midterm elections. Trump has embarked on a frenzied schedule of campaign rallies in the final stretch to juice enthusiasm among the Republican faithful, but with a historically low approval rating and growing voter frustration about high prices, he and the Republican Party face major political headwinds.

The president has been calling friends, White House aides and outside advisers because he appears worried that information is not reaching him, according to an adviser who received one of the calls. In these conversations, he has also vented about the midterms and the two outside advisers quarterbacking his political strategy, James Blair and Chris LaCivita, who are close allies of Wiles.

Among those who have been in contact with Trump is former aide Corey Lewandowski, a fierce rival of Wiles's, who is supportive of Pulte, according to two people with knowledge of the conversations.

Reached for comment, Lewandowski said: "I have never spoken with the president about Bill Pulte being the chief of staff."

"These anonymous sources know nothing. It's the same selfish, opportunistic behavior from people more focused on themselves than on President Trump, whose priority is delivering for the American people and winning the midterms," Danielle Alvarez, a White House spokesperson, said in response to a request for comment. "President Trump has assembled a strong, talented and united team focused on his America First agenda - not the egos and political games of anonymous outsiders."

Internal GOP polling shows that support for Republican candidates cratered after the party's midterm convention in Dallas, with voters saying the party was not attuned to their economic concerns, according to a Republican strategist briefed on the numbers. Rather than campaigning extensively in September, Trump spent much of the month hosting Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House and working on his construction projects, including a new White House helipad and his proposed ballroom.

Although the White House continues to express confidence in public, many Trump aides and allies believe they will lose control of the House of Representatives, although by how large a margin remains unclear. Trump advisers and Republican strategists say the fate of the Senate is a 50-50 proposition, despite a deluge of spending in recent weeks by the president's main super PAC, MAGA Inc., and the Senate Leadership Fund. They acknowledge that typically red states, including Kansas and Texas, are in play.

Whether Wiles will opt to stay in her position if the midterms yield major GOP losses has emerged as a dominant topic in Trumpworld.

A Republican "blowout next month, very likely, will be a wedge that the ambitious use" to slide into the chief of staff's office, one Wiles ally said.

The jockeying to become the next chief of staff has taken various forms. Pulte frequently lugs poster boards onto the golf course, Marine One or Air Force One to try to nudge Trump to sign on to his ideas.

Typically, the poster boards contain Pulte's proposals to handle whatever issue is irking the president that day - be it the renovations to the Kennedy Center or the Federal Reserve's failure to lower interest rates. Sometimes the posters include artwork of the president, or images of his rallies, according to one person who has viewed the posters. Trump's love of visual aids has its limits; he has told advisers that Pulte has brought him so many poster boards that they are cluttering up the White House residence, said two White House officials and a third person close to the White House.

Wiles ran Trump's highly disciplined 2024 presidential campaign and paved the way for him and his team to take swift action through more than 100 executive orders during his first 100 days in office. While she does not consider herself a policy expert, she has inserted herself into the center of the administration's debates on global tariffs and potential guardrails for artificial intelligence, as both became political liabilities for the president.

But Wiles and her inner circle were put on the defensive recently after Blair and LaCivita traveled to Republika Srpska - the Serbian-dominated portion of Bosnia - to do political consulting work for the pro-Russian government.

That created problems for Wiles, who had brought both men into Trump's 2024 campaign. The president has always bristled when current or former aides profit off their connections to him.

Trump responded by posting a pointed message on Truth Social distancing himself from Blair and LaCivita and promising to fire them if their consulting work posed a conflict of interest.

The story got worse for the chief of staff when a photo surfaced of her daughter, Katie Wiles, on a visit to Republika Srpska. The younger Wiles is a partner at the lobbying firm Continental Strategy, which represents the territory's government (though she is not individually named on the firm's lobbying disclosure forms). Detractors of Wiles, LaCivita and Blair have been fueling the tensions and stoking Trump's suspicions by showing him critical articles about the foreign consulting, three outside advisers said.

Blair and LaCivita are still leading Trump's midterm strategy, and the president still talks to Blair frequently, but his initial unhappiness with their trip may have weakened the duo's ability to offer guidance and issue directives to various campaigns, one Republican strategist said.

data.title: The U.S. economy is facing 2 hot wars heating up at a bad time for the White House
data.description:
The US economy is facing 2 hot wars heating up at a bad time for the White House

Jake Conley and Michael B. Kelley
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 4:01 AM PDT 6 min read

Yields are above multidecade highs, both gas and diesel prices continue to climb, and critical midterm elections are around the corner.

Adding to pressure on the US economy and the current administration, the world's two largest hot wars are heating up.

'Iran knows when the midterms are too'

In the Middle East, dual fronts along the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea have seen a resurgence of conflict in recent weeks that has heavily disrupted oil flows in the region.

Multiple tankers and container ships in the Strait of Hormuz either caught fire or sank this week in the Iran-dominated waterway. The Washington Institute has tracked more than two dozen attacks recorded since the start of the month.

President Trump has said the US military won't resume airstrikes inside Iran before the midterm elections as White House negotiators continue angling for a diplomatic solution to the conflict now in its eighth month.

Read more: How to protect your money as Mideast turmoil fuels market volatility

At the same time, administration officials are reportedly war-gaming a major offensive to come after the November elections, when the president will be less encumbered by the political needs of the Republican Party.

"The Trump Administration does not want Brent crude oil at $106/bbl going into the midterm elections, just a month away, and has said that he only plans to escalate offenses against Iran after the midterms are over, with what he hopes to be, a red wave," Rabobank cross-asset macro strategist Molly Schwartz said in a recent note to clients.

To the west along the Red Sea, Yemen's Houthi militants have sharply escalated their campaign against the Saudi coalition opposing the group's bid for wider territorial control, launching multiple rounds of strikes on major airports inside the kingdom that have killed more than a dozen people and wounded hundreds.

Houthi militants recently struck an office building belonging to the state-managed oil giant Saudi Aramco (2223.SR). While the kingdom's oil production remains largely undisrupted, violent pestering by the Iran-allied Houthis is driving up oil prices.

"Iran knows when the midterms are too," Schwartz added, "and if they want to further complicate Trump's plans, now is the perfect time to have the Houthis stir up trouble and make it increasingly difficult for the US to avoid intervening."

Ukraine, Russia, and Starlink throttling

Ukraine and Russia, which have been at war since Russia executed a stealth annexation of Crimea in 2014 and invaded its neighbor in February 2022, recently both escalated offensive strikes against critical infrastructure ahead of another winter.

Kyiv leverages long-range drone attacks to knock out oil refineries inside Russia, claiming to have disrupted half the country's refining capacity, while Moscow has repeatedly targeted power plants and other civilian infrastructure inside Ukraine.

Over the weekend, President Trump called for an "energy ceasefire," part of a bid to bring down US diesel prices that has included a deal that will see the US buy Russian fuel, breaking with several years of sanctions meant to pressure the Kremlin's war chest.

Shortly after the announcement, Russia launched a round of strikes against power plants in Ukraine, prompting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to say Kyiv would continue to target Russian refineries.

On Wednesday, Ukraine reported rate-throttling of Starlink, satellite communications services developed by SpaceX (SPCX), and its military subscription service StarShield.

On Thursday evening, citing an official familiar with the matter, Reuters reported that "the order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House."

Ukrainian troops use both Starlink and Starshield terminals.

Oil prices and yields pressure US economy

Taken together, the conflicts are putting immense pressure on the global energy system — and, increasingly, on the US economy.

While oil exports from the Persian Gulf have returned to prewar levels via alternative routes, exports through the waterway itself — which before the war accounted for roughly one-fifth of global oil flows — have remained far below prewar levels.

And prior to 2022, Russia provided roughly 10% of the world's diesel exports. But Moscow has largely been cut off from the market after international sanctions and domestic export bans.

The US economy is feeling the disruption: Yields on US 10-year and 30-year Treasurys have climbed to levels not seen since the early 2000s, pressuring consumer and corporate borrowers. Gasoline and diesel prices have soared to record levels.

Recent reports from the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed inflation readings on both consumer and producer prices accelerating faster than expected, with energy prices rising at the quickest pace since March, just after the start of the Iran war.

For the White House, those economic pressures have complicated the outlook for midterm elections less than three weeks away.

In comments to reporters on Wednesday night, President Trump said again that the war in Iran will "end very soon," and the White House is reportedly considering the use of a GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB) — the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal, which would mark a major step-up in escalation.

Iran is not backing down: Parliamentary speaker Mohamed Bagher Ghalibaf said on Wednesday that Iran will fight until its demands are met in negotiations.

In Ukraine, President Zelensky has ordered renewed attacks on Russian refineries.

And with only a few short weeks left until the midterms, the reheating of both wars has left the White House — and, by proxy, the US economy — between a rock and a hard place.

Jake Conley is a breaking news reporter covering US equities for Yahoo Finance. Follow him on X at @byjakeconley or email him at jake.conley@yahooinc.com.

data.title: 'You should be ashamed of yourself': Heated Senate debates become personal
data.description:
Video Ad Feedback
Protester interrupts Maine Senate debate and confronts GOP Sen. Collins on data centers
0:33 • Source: CNN
Protester interrupts Maine Senate debate and confronts GOP Sen. Collins on data centers
0:33
See all topics
Email
Link Copied!

Candidates faced off in heated debates Thursday night in two of the country’s most competitive Senate races, showing how bitter — and personal — each contest has become.

In Maine, Democratic nominee Troy Jackson told GOP Sen. Susan Collins to “shut up” after she suggested a protester was one of his supporters. And in Alaska, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan questioned Democratic opponent Mary Peltola’s “character” while citing allegations she mistreated staff.

“I think that Alaskans have had it up to here with the lying and dishonesty,” Peltola said during another exchange. “Dan, you should be ashamed of yourself.”

The races are unfolding thousands of miles apart but both critical to the Senate majority. Collins, a moderate Republican, is seeking reelection in a blue state, while Sullivan is running for another term in more GOP-leaning Alaska where Peltola, a former congresswoman, is well-known.

Both debates showed how much of a political liability President Donald Trump’s war in Iran has become for Republican incumbents. Sullivan said it “needs to end soon,” while Collins continued to insist Trump should have consulted Congress on the conflict.

Here’s a look at key moments from the debates.

US Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic candidate for the US Senate Troy Jackson are seen during their debate at the Gracie Theatre in Bangor, Maine on Thursday.

A protester disrupts Collins on data centers

The fourth and final Senate debate in Maine grew heated as Collins and Jackson sharpened their attacks.

Within minutes, a protester shouted at Collins about the impact of data centers, forcing the debate to a brief halt.

“AI data centers are destroying our climate. They are poisoning our waters,” the protester yelled.

Following the incident, Collins said the protester “is obviously one of Troy’s supporters.”

“Oh, shut up,” Jackson replied, saying he did not know who the person was.

Corruption allegations and campaign financing in Maine

During the Collins-Jackson debate, both candidates tried to portray their opponent as corrupt, a major theme that has loomed over the hotly contested race and the midterms nationally.

Collins cornered Jackson for not sharing his FEC report with her on Wednesday, a promise he made at their debate earlier this week.

Jackson said he missed his self-imposed deadline because it took longer to process the donations from 200,000 people to his campaign than he expected.

“I had to make sure this report was right. It was my first one,” Jackson said.

Throughout the campaign, Jackson has framed Collins as being influenced by her donors and touted that he doesn’t take any corporate PAC money. Collins tried to flip the script on Thursday by dinging Jackson for running joint ads with his party’s Senate campaign arm, which does take money from corporations, and for not disclosing his donors.

Jackson said he did not control their donations to the Senate campaign committee but did concede his campaign has taken money from billionaires.

“That is accurate. But I haven’t made any deals like Senator Collins has with those billionaires. I don’t owe them any votes. I am going to tax those billionaires when I get to the US Senate. So, if they want to give me money during this campaign, I guess that’s up to them,” Jackson said.

When it was Jackson’s turn to ask Collins a question, he got personal. In defending his credentials and pushing back on Collins’ critique that he doesn’t have the right experience, Jackson exclaimed, “Is it just me that you look down on or is it working-class people overall?”

Collins further distances from Trump on Iran war

Collins doubled down on her criticism of the Iran war as the Maine Republican continues to distance herself from Trump.

When asked if Congress should have been consulted before Trump decided to go to war, Collins said, “Congress definitely should have been consulted.”

But Collins added that that the War Powers Resolution gave Trump the flexibility to act unilaterally within the first 60 days of the conflict, which she said is why she did not start voting to rein in Trump’s war powers until after those initial 60 days had passed.

Video Ad Feedback
Sullivan and Peltola clash in Alaska race that could decide Senate control
0:36 • Source: CNN
Sullivan and Peltola clash in Alaska race that could decide Senate control
0:36

Iran war’s consequences also hangs over Alaska debate

Sullivan repeatedly had to grapple with issues where Trump has not made the race easy for him. The war in Iran, for example, has led to especially high fuel costs in Alaska.

Sullivan said he has opposed limiting Trump’s Iran powers because he supports the overall goal of preventing the country from obtaining a nuclear weapon. But he said the war “needs to end soon.”

“The energy costs from this war are too high, but … the best way to bring down costs with regard to energy in Alaska is to produce more energy by and for Alaskans,” Sullivan said, suggesting Peltola could not be trusted to support that.

Peltola blamed Washington politicians for “waging forever wars that are skyrocketing our costs.” And she scoffed at Sullivan’s pivot to the topic of domestic energy production.

“I have been a strong supporter of drilling in Alaska,” she said. “That is not the issue here.”

Sullivan continued to show daylight with Trump when asked about Trump’s plan to buy Russian diesel. He reiterated his opposition, saying, “I don’t think it’s a good ideal at all,” and noting he “just led the effort” to pass new sanctions on Russia in Congress.

Sullivan, Peltola spar over her treatment of staff

Sullivan and Peltola clashed twice over a September story from The New York Times that alleged staff mistreatment by Peltola. In the article, her campaign pushed back on the suggestion she regularly abused her staff but said she occasionally “struggled to deal with her grief” after her mother and husband died in 2023.

“I do not think that this election is about me on my worst day, and I found so many of these allegations concerning and outright fabrications or mass exaggerations of the truth,” Peltola said at the debate when asked about the Times report.

Sullivan emphasized that the story was based on interviews with nine former staff members and at least 20 other people.

“It’s not Mary Peltola on her worst day,” Sullivan said. “It’s Mary Peltola over the course of a couple years with dozens of people weighing in on this.”

Sullivan brought up the Times story on his own earlier in the debate, saying Peltola has “treated young Alaskans horribly” and that it was “a character flaw.” Peltola called it “gossip” and “unfounded allegations” as Sullivan talked over her.

“It’s the New York Times,” he said. “Read the article.”

Sullivan questions whether Peltola got questions in advance

The Times story was not the only cause for animosity between the two candidates.

After Peltola criticized Sullivan about the war in Iran, looking down at notes on her podium as she spoke, Sullivan turned to the moderators.

“We weren’t supposed to get these questions beforehand were, we?” he asked.

“No, sir,” one moderator said before another added: “Neither one of you got questions beforehand. Absolutely not.”

“OK,” Sullivan said. “I’m just watching my opponent read from questions that seem to be answered.”

“I’m prepared,” Peltola said.

Sullivan appeared to back down from his suggestion while speaking with reporters after the debate, according to Alaska Public Media, which quoted him telling the hosts, “I’m not blaming you guys.”

data.title: The midterm polls are predicting a blue wave. Can they be trusted?
data.description:
The 2026 midterms polls are predicting a blue wave. Can they be trusted?

After major misses in recent elections, some experts say there's reason to look at polls predicting a Democratic landslide with a healthy dose of skepticism.

Mike Bebernes, Andrew Romano
Thu, October 15, 2026 at 8:13 PM UTC
11 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Anyone who's followed American politics over the past decade or so has learned to look at political polls with a healthy dose of skepticism. Some of the most important recent elections have featured substantial polling errors that left many Americans baffled when things turned out differently than they expected.

As we head into a pivotal midterm election, the polls are generally telling the same story. Forecasts point to the possibility of a blue wave that will sweep across the country, likely allowing Democrats to flip control of the House of Representatives and giving them a chance of gaining a majority in the Senate as well. 

Is that story true, though? We won't know for certain until after the actual votes are counted, but there is evidence that can give us a slightly better sense of what the polls are seeing, what they might be missing and how well other political trends match the picture that the polls are painting.

What the polls say

In a midterm election, there are three types of polls to watch if you want a sense of where things stand in the battle for control of Congress.

Advertisement

The first tracks the approval rating of someone who isn't even on the ballot in November: the president of the United States. Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. (The average number lost since World War II? Twenty-six.) Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses seats across a wide range of competitive districts — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election.

Knowing how Americans feel about the president's job performance is helpful because they tend to channel those feelings into their votes for the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives. Right now, 60% of Americans, on average, disapprove of how President Trump is handling his job, according to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin; 38% approve. That puts the president's net disapproval rating at about 22 percentage points. 

Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top issue this year: the cost of living. Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today — as tariffs and the Iran war help drive prices up — 71% disapprove and 25% approve. That's a 46-point gap.

The second type of poll to pay attention to is what's known (at least among politics nerds) as the "generic ballot," which typically asks something along the lines of: If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? This is our best measure of how partisan sentiment is shaping up across all 435 U.S. House contests. At the moment, Democrats have a lead on the generic ballot — nearly 9 percentage points, on average — and Republican support has been trending downward since September.

To put that in perspective, Democrats were leading by an average of 7 points on the generic ballot at this point in 2018, with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate. Three weeks later, Democrats picked up 41 seats and flipped the House. (This year, Democrats need to net only three seats to win control of that chamber.)

The third and final type of polling that matters in a congressional midterm cycle is state surveys of key Senate contests. Here's where the data gets a little trickier. In recent weeks, the preponderance of polling has shown Democrats widening their leads in competitive states where they're defending seats they already hold (Georgia, Minnesota, New Hampshire, Michigan) while also gaining ground in red states where they're trying to flip a Republican-held seat (Alaska, Iowa, Texas, Kansas, Ohio). 

Some Republicans are arguing that this red-state Senate polling could be inaccurate — and pointing to past polling "misses" to make their case.

How badly have polls missed in the past?

It's important to note that polling errors should be expected in any race. Polling is an inexact science. No matter how sophisticated a pollster's process is, it invariably includes assumptions, adjustments and extrapolations that leave a lot of room for error. That uncertainty has been a feature of election polling throughout its history.

Those misses are less impactful in years where the variance in polls balances out. If they underestimate the Republicans' strength in some races while overselling the GOP in others, you end up with polling that generally reflects the actual results in the aggregate.

The problem over the past decade is that, in multiple elections, the polls have mostly missed in the same direction. 

Trump's win over Hillary Clinton in 2016 came as such a surprise because polls had systematically underestimated his support. When it came to the national popular vote, the polls were relatively accurate. The big misses came in the swing states that decided the election. Heading into Election Day, polls showed Clinton ahead — sometimes by a large margin — in five states that Trump ended up winning. The 2016 election sparked a reckoning within the polling world. The major polling firms realized that something had made them underestimate the size of Trump's voting coalition. They spent years making changes to how they collect and interpret data to fix that clear blind spot. 

Things looked more promising after the 2018 midterms. The polls were reasonably accurate. When they did miss, they missed in both directions, meaning the polls weren't systematically biased against either party. 

Then came 2020. Even though the polls accurately predicted Joe Biden would win, they underestimated Republicans' support by even more than they had four years earlier. Trump performed nearly 3 percentage points better than expected in the national popular vote and outperformed polls in individual states by more than 4 points. The miss was even bigger in Senate and gubernatorial races.

The polls bounced back in 2022, when they were more accurate than in any election in recent history, before once again underestimating Republicans in 2024 — though by a smaller margin than in either 2016 or 2020.

The pattern over the past decade has been that polls have tended to be biased against Republicans when Trump is on the ballot and reasonably on point when he's not. While that could be considered reason for optimism among Democrats, five election cycles is hardly a definitive sample.

Why the polls might be wrong

A lot of explanations have been put forward to try to understand the polling misses in recent presidential elections. The most commonly cited is the belief that MAGA Republicans, due to their general lack of trust in mainstream institutions, are less likely to pick up the phone when a polling firm calls than members of other political groups. That phenomenon, which pollsters call "nonresponse bias," can skew survey samples and make the share of Republican voters appear smaller than it really is. 

"The polling is wrong. ... Republicans don't want to respond to polls anymore," House Speaker Mike Johnson told Fox News on Tuesday. 

Johnson and other Republicans have pointed to some surprising survey results on the Senate side to bolster their argument that polls might be missing GOP voters. That includes Democratic leads and strong showings by independents in Senate races in deep red states like Iowa, Kansas and Nebraska. For those polls to be accurate, voter sentiment would have had to have swung as much as 23 points in Democrats' direction since the last midterm Senate contests in those states. 

One pollster recently described GOP voters' nonresponse in a poll they conducted in Iowa as a "canary in the cornfields" for a potentially widespread undercounting of Republican support in the state.

Polling firms try to account for nonresponse bias by adjusting their results to give less weight to people from groups who are overrepresented in their samples, but doing so means making a lot of assumptions about the nature of a constantly evolving electorate. It's possible that the adjustments they're making this year aren't enough to accurately reflect voters' sentiments. 

On top of gauging how people will vote, there's also the challenge of determining who will vote. Polls often include results for "likely" voters — voters who are expected to cast a ballot — but deciding who should fit into that category involves its own assumptions that can be wrong. Earlier this month, the polling firm YouGov released a survey showing Democrats up 16 points nationally with likely voters, a gap that YouGov itself described as "hard-to-believe." 

While the major recent polling errors have been in presidential election years, data compiled by Republican pollster Patrick Ruffini suggests that the polls have also had some noteworthy misses in midterm cycles as well. 

"Nationally, the polls were pretty good, but red state polls were too blue and blue state polls too red," he wrote on X.

If Ruffini's analysis is accurate, that could mean that Democrats' chances of flipping Senate seats in states like Texas, Iowa and Ohio aren't nearly as strong as they appear to be. 

Republicans also have more room for error in the House this year thanks to redistricting. The GOP's sweeping campaign to redraw congressional maps in red states gave them up to nine new safe House seats. Democrats tried to even the score by doing their own gerrymandering. But when the dust settled, Republicans still came out ahead.

That said, Republicans might still struggle to keep their majority in the House even if the polls are off by a significant margin. On the other hand, when it comes to the Senate, the polls would only need to be off by a few points in a handful of key states for the GOP to maintain control over the chamber. 

Why the polls might be right

Polling errors are commonplace; they happen in most elections. But they tend to be random and to change directions from one cycle to another. 

The argument that skeptics are making this time around is that there is something fundamentally different about the Trump era — something that systematically skews all poll results involving Trump.

This has been true, to a degree, in each of the three presidential contests that Trump himself has competed in. There, the final average of polls conducted before Election Day underestimated Republicans' performance in the popular vote by an average of 3.8 percentage points, according to data journalist Nate Silver. 

But there has been no systematic polling bias toward Democrats in Trump-era elections when Trump himself was not on the ballot. In fact, the polls since 2016 have overestimated Republican support in midterm elections (by an average of 0.2%) and off-year, special and runoff elections (by an average of 1.3%), according to Silver. 

One possible explanation for this dynamic is that "the midterm electorate skews toward politically engaged voters who are more trusting of institutions and more likely to have answered polls," as the Atlantic recently put it. To be significantly wrong in 2026, the polls would have to be wrong in ways they weren't in 2022 and 2018. 

There are other reasons to believe the polls could be right as well. While there are signs that rural Republicans are not responding to pollsters in certain states, that doesn't necessarily mean that those voters are secretly planning to show up and surprise everyone on Election Day. Instead, experts say that it might mean the opposite: that they don't want to answer questions about politics because they are not particularly enthusiastic about voting this year. Pollsters aren't seeing this "rural nonresponse" effect everywhere, either. 

The parties are also behaving as if the polls are accurate. Republicans' spending patterns show that they are "pour[ing] money into dozens of U.S. House races previously considered 'safe,'" Reuters recently reported. Democrats are also campaigning hard in parts of the country that would typically be out of their reach.  

Meanwhile, "some top congressional Republicans have privately concluded that it is likely impossible for them to keep control of the House of Representatives in the midterm elections," according to Politico. 

On the Senate side, the major GOP campaign groups have reportedly cut back on spending in North Carolina and Georgia, a sign that they may be losing faith in winning those races, and rerouted the money to defend a historically safe seat in Kansas. 

None of this guarantees that the polls are right. They could be rife with the same errors that have plagued them in recent elections, or have new blind spots that won't become clear until later. However, the polls currently reflect what you might expect to see in a political environment in which historical precedent suggests the party in power will struggle, the president's approval rating is low, and the parties are battling it out in what are normally deep red parts of the country.

We'll find out just how accurate the polls really are on Nov. 3.

data.title: Trump calls Ukraine's renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries 'a disgrace'
data.description:
Trump calls Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries ‘a disgrace’

Jennifer Rankin in Brussels and agencies
Fri, 16 October 2026 at 10:01 am UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Donald Trump has called Ukraine's renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries "a disgrace" and criticised Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy after an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.

Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries ⁠after Zelenskyy said Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire unilaterally declared by Trump on Sunday, having briefly halted its attacks to demonstrate its readiness for peace talks. Russia had continued its strikes on Ukrainian power plants.

Related: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump 'energy ceasefire' collapses

Advertisement

In an interview with Newsmax aired on Thursday, the US president said: "All he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace.

"There are a lot ‌of targets you can ‌hit, but when you shoot at diesel refineries where you make, you know, ‌diesel oil, and we need that, and the world needs that, then he's not doing a good service for the world."

Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since Trump announced an easing sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel on to global markets.

Zelenskyy criticised the agreement, which was widely interpreted as an attempt to curb high fuel prices before the US midterm elections, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than four and a half years ago. US efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.

Advertisement

Trump repeated to Newsmax his views of the two leaders involved in the conflict. "I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Trump said. "I think they actually both would like to see it ⁠end, but I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult ​to deal with ​than Putin."

Arriving in Brussels to meet EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy did not comment on Trump's latest remarks. He said he was "so thankful that we have such huge support from the EU" and its leaders, whom he described as "real leaders".

He went on to say that Ukraine wanted to end the war as quickly as possible, but "we don't see now signals from [the] Russian side that they are ready for this".

Kyiv's relationship with Washington was strained further this week when Ukraine said Starlink services had been restricted, in effect hobbling Ukrainian drone strike missions and crucial air defences with a flick of the switch.

Advertisement

During a visit to London this week, the Ukrainian president said the sudden restriction of Starlink had left him feeling personally betrayed by Trump and lamented losing a partner.

Related: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump 'energy ceasefire' collapses

The British defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said on Thursday that his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, had assured him in a face-to-face meeting that the vital satellite communications system had been restored. In an interview with the BBC, he said it was unclear what had caused the disruption, but added: "This is not the first time we've seen a falling out between Washington and Kyiv."

Amid growing doubts about long-term US commitment to Ukraine, European leaders declared their support for Zelenskyy.

Advertisement

Standing alongside the Ukrainian leader in Brussels, the European Council president, António Costa, said Ukraine could "count on us not only to support you in war" but also in the path to negotiating EU membership.

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU had supported Trump's energy ceasefire, "but we have seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute" and instead had escalated its attacks. She said the EU intended to increase pressure on Russia, promising a 22nd round of sanctions, adding: "We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war."

The promise of further European sanctions against Russia comes weeks after the EU lifted sanctions against two prominent Russian oligarchs at the request of France and Luxembourg.

After meeting Zelenskyy, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, said it was "crucial" that Ukraine received "all the means necessary to protect itself".

Advertisement

The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, posted online: "I can reassure you, dear Ukrainian friends and President Zelenskyy: YOU ARE NOT ALONE."

As Zelenskyy met Macron in Brussels, he said that the Kremlin had "launched yet another vile drone strike on Ukrainian energy infrastructure" in the city of Lutsk, which caused blackouts.

The Kremlin, meanwhile, accused Ukraine of derailing US peace efforts by resuming its strikes on refineries.

data.title: Ousted general warned of missile defense shortage before Iran war
data.description:
Exclusive
Politics

Ousted general warned of years-long missile defense shortage before Iran war

By
James LaPorta
National Security Coordinating Producer
James LaPorta is a coordinating producer for the CBS News national security team. He's a former U.S. Marine and veteran of the Afghanistan war.
Read Full Bio
James LaPorta

Updated on: October 15, 2026 / 4:39 PM EDT / CBS News

Add CBS News on Google

Washington — In late December, two months before the U.S. war with Iran began, Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George warned that his service was critically short on missile defense munitions and that the shortage would last another five years, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the matter. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ousted George in April, as the Iran war was underway.

George's risk analysis appeared in the Pentagon's Global Force Management Allocation Plan, a defense secretary-approved annual order determining where  troops and weapons will be allocated across the globe, according to the U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News. 

He warned that the stockpile of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense batteries and Patriot missiles would continue to be strategically low until 2030. His assessment was written for the Defense Department's plan for fiscal year 2027 and before the outbreak of the U.S.-Israel-led war with Iran, now in its seventh month. 

U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly said his assessment stemmed from the transfer of Patriots to Ukraine after Russia's invasion in 2022, the expenditure of munitions to defend Israel, and the reduced capacity of the defense industrial base. 

CBS News is withholding the exact percentage figures conveyed by U.S. officials because of security concerns, and George declined to comment. U.S. officials say  that while the U.S. possesses a significant stockpile of some offensive munitions, like the Joint Direct Attack Munition and Small Diameter Bombs, missile defense munitions used in Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, batteries, and Patriot missile systems are at low strategic-risk levels. 

The THAAD system is one of the U.S. military's most advanced missile defense systems, designed to intercept and destroy incoming ballistic missiles during the final phase of their flight, either inside or just outside Earth's atmosphere. The Army has eight THAAD batteries. Each battery consists of 90 soldiers who operate six truck-mounted launchers, with each truck possessing eight launchers. A full battery controls 48 interceptors, according to a 2025 report from the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service. 

The Patriot air-defense system is designed to protect military installations, troops and other critical infrastructure from incoming ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as hostile aircraft. It can engage a broader range of aerial threats at lower altitudes than a THAAD battery, but when used together, they provide even more effective overlapping layers of defense against missile attacks. 

The Patriot munition at a critical low is the Patriot Advanced Capability-3, or PAC-3, a high-velocity surface-to-air interceptor designed to destroy incoming tactical ballistic missiles and cruise missiles by ramming into them. PAC-3s can also bring down enemy aircraft, according to U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News. 

"Those are the two Army munitions that would be most heavily used in a conflict with China," said Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and CSIS Defense and Security senior adviser. "You're not gonna use that many Javelins, for example, because the amount of ground combat is going to be relatively limited, even artillery will be limited, but air defense — missile defense — that will be huge." 

An April estimate from the Center for Strategic and International Studies showed that it currently takes defense contractors four years and five months to complete delivery of new THAAD interceptor contracts. Patriot PAC-3 interceptor orders have an average delivery time of three and a half years. 

CSIS' estimate said that before the Iran war, the U.S. entered 2026 with roughly 2,300 or so Patriot interceptors and expended between 1,050 and 1,430 during the conflict, potentially consuming as much as 61% of its prewar inventory. Fewer than 500 replenishment munitions were expected to be delivered in fiscal year 2026. 

The stockpile for THAAD systems prior to the Iran war sat at around 355 interceptors, with the Iran war using between 190 to 290, or about 82% of its prewar inventory, according to CSIS. There were no expected deliveries for replenishment in fiscal year 2026. In the current fiscal year — 2027 — the U.S. has requested more than 800 THAADs. 

Two of the nation's largest defense contractors — Lockheed Martin and RTX, through its Raytheon business — are involved in manufacturing these systems and their key components. They've recently signed agreements aimed at accelerating production. 

In January, Lockheed Martin announced a plan to quadruple the production capacity of THAADs from 96 to 400 interceptors per year. 

While the war with Iran has caused missile defense munitions to be depleted at a much higher rate, decades of Pentagon spending decisions, a shrinking defense industrial base and successive military operations that consume weapons faster than manufacturers can replace them have contributed to the current shortages.

One U.S. official told CBS News that even if the United States could avoid expending additional THAAD or Patriot munitions in Iran or in other conflicts, it would take until the midterm elections of the next presidential administration — 2030 — to replenish the stockpile to the already-low December 2025 levels. 

Contacted by CBS News, Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell said, "Claims of U.S. munitions shortages are false. When the Fake News media irresponsibly amplifies these lies, the real-world consequences is clear: our enemies are emboldened to provide — or attack — American troops."

He added that the U.S. still has  "everything required to strike at the time and place of the President's choosing." 

"Across multiple combatant commands," Parnell said, "we have already executed successful operations while maintaining a deep, ready arsenal to defend our people and our interests."

How munitions are used around the world 

The U.S. military is divided into 11 unified combatant commands, each responsible for either a region of the world or specialized military mission. For operations against Iran, U.S. Central Command, led by Navy Adm. Brad Cooper, is in charge. 

Each combatant command needs a certain number of troops and weapons. The Pentagon uses a framework known as Global Force Management to decide where American troops, their units and some of the military's most sought-after weapons are sent around the world. 

The Global Force Management Allocation Plan, or GFMAP, is at the center of the process, laying out which forces will be provided to combatant commanders, for what missions and for how long. 

The plan is typically organized around the federal fiscal year. Generally, the Pentagon enters a new fiscal year with an existing plan for many of the forces expected to deploy or remain deployed during the coming 12 to 24 months, rather than deciding from scratch each time a commander asks for troops or weapons. 

But the plan is not set in stone. Wars erupt, crises develop, missions end and commanders are faced with unanticipated events to address.

For instance, the commander of U.S. European Command might want more Patriots in Poland at the same time that U.S. Central Command wants those same resources in Kuwait, while U.S. Indo-Pacific Command may also need the systems for contingencies involving China. 

There's a constant shuffling of troops and assets from one region to another — in one instance in April 2025, Adm. Samuel Paparo, the commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, told the Senate Armed Services Committee that the Army had transferred a Patriot battalion from his region to U.S. Central Command amid ongoing fighting with the Iranian-back Houthi rebels in Yemen. 

What led to the current weapons systems shortage?

After the collapse of the Soviet Union, American military planners abandoned the assumption that the U.S. might need to fight a prolonged war against another superpower, explained Cancian. 

"After the Cold War, we planned on fighting short regional conflicts against countries like Iraq or North Korea. And for those countries we didn't need the large inventories that we had needed during the Cold War," Cancian said. "We needed much smaller inventories." 

He added: "We shrank the industrial base. There was the famous 'Last Supper' which was literally a dinner that the deputy defense secretary put on for the heads of the defense industry, and he told them there's not enough money to keep you all in business, so you're going to have to consolidate or move out of the business, which they did." 

The resulting mergers reduced the number of major aerospace and defense contractors from 51 to five, according to the CSIS analysis. 

Also, historically, the Pentagon's procurement decisions have reduced spending on ammunition and missiles to free up money for fighter jets, tanks and warships, even while acknowledging that those weapons are essential to war fighting.  

Cancian told CBS News that the consolidation of the defense industrial base shaped an industry that produces efficiently during peacetime but is not designed to surge production. 

"We squeezed all the surge out because it was seen as unnecessary. So, that's where we end up when the war in Ukraine begins," said Cancian. "And after six months or so, we realized that we just don't have enough munitions and equipment for a protracted conflict." 

Under the Biden administration, there was a renewed interest in building surge capabilities back into the defense industrial base but that would take time. As the war between Russia and Ukraine began in full, the U.S. transferred roughly 600 Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine. However, not all of those weapons came from American military stockpiles; some were manufactured through the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative or provided by European countries. 

Additionally, both Biden and Trump administrations used Patriot and THAAD missile interceptors to defend Israel against Iranian strikes. Six months before Gen. George's warning assessment, U.S. forces fired roughly 150 THAAD interceptors and almost 80 Patriot interceptors during the Twelve Day War. 

Cancian noted that the five-year timeline to bring Patriot and THAAD stockpiles just to the low pre-Iran war levels is based on the assumption that the production schedule stays on track — and that additional military operations do not further deplete the inventory. 

This story published first on CBS News at 4:28 p.m. on Oct. 15, 2026.
